title: United States v. Richardson
lead: Richardson sought a public account of intelligence expenditures, but the Supreme Court held that his taxpayer and voting interests did not give him standing to challenge the secrecy provisions.

actors.name: Richardson
actors.role: Taxpayer, citizen, and voter seeking intelligence-expenditure information.

actors.name: Treasury’s Bureau of Accounts
actors.role: Office that supplied general financial reports but no additional intelligence figures.

actors.name: Central Intelligence Agency
actors.role: Agency permitted by statute to account for specified expenditures through its Director’s certificate.

proceedings: The district court dismissed for lack of standing and political-question concerns; the en banc Third Circuit reversed. The Supreme Court reversed the Third Circuit, 5–4, solely on standing.
limits: The constitutional validity of the accounting statute, the Statement and Account Clause’s precise requirements, and the political-question issue were not decided. Brennan’s applicable dissent appears in the companion Schlesinger report.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Richardson asks where the intelligence figures are
paragraphs: Richardson wanted to know the Central Intelligence Agency’s expenditures. In 1967 he requested the documents published under Article I, § 9, clause 7 of the Constitution, which required periodic statements and accounts of public receipts and expenditures. Treasury’s Bureau of Accounts supplied its Combined Statement and monthly and daily reports.

Richardson then asked how the Central Intelligence Agency Act’s special accounting provisions could be reconciled with the statement’s authenticity and how to obtain the missing figures. The Bureau had no further information. Treasury also declined to ask the Attorney General for an opinion on the statute’s constitutionality. The challenged provision allowed expenditures to be accounted for solely on the agency Director’s certificate.

sections.title: He turns the denied request into a constitutional suit
paragraphs: Suing as a taxpayer, Richardson alleged that the Government offered a fraudulent substitute for the constitutionally required account. He requested a permanent injunction against publishing the Combined Statement as compliance until it actually met the constitutional obligation. He also asserted interests as a citizen and voter: without expenditure information he could not properly evaluate government and electoral candidates. These were claimed informational and political injuries, not findings that intelligence money had been misused.

The district court dismissed under the taxpayer-standing decision Flast v. Cohen and also considered the dispute a political question. It initially declined to convene a three-judge court. The en banc Third Circuit, with three dissenters, reversed and directed consideration by a three-judge court. It reasoned that accounting was integrally linked to appropriations because Richardson could not challenge expenditures he could not see. The Supreme Court later observed that his complaint did not announce the later appropriations challenge that this theory appeared to anticipate.

sections.title: The majority treats the claim as outside the taxpayer exception
paragraphs: Chief Justice Burger wrote for Justices White, Blackmun, Powell, and Rehnquist. The earlier Frothingham decision rejected federal taxpayer suits resting on an indefinite interest in the treasury. Flast created a narrow exception requiring a connection both to a challenged congressional exercise of taxing and spending and to a specific constitutional restriction on that power. It did not license every taxpayer objection to government, and Article III still required a personal stake producing concrete adversity.

Richardson challenged accounting and reporting arrangements, not an exercise of taxing and spending alleged to violate a specific restriction on that power. Seeking information about expenditures did not supply the missing nexus. The majority considered the nature of the claim to determine standing while expressly reserving its constitutional merits. Other agencies’ confidential reporting provisions and Congress’s combination of broader disclosure under the Freedom of Information Act with confidentiality protections supplied context, not approval of all secrecy restrictions.

sections.title: A shared voting concern does not produce a judicial remedy
sections.cue: The majority’s further reasoning and judgment
paragraphs: The majority also found no particular concrete injury in Richardson’s claimed inability to evaluate officials, executive activity, and candidates. That concern was common to the public and thus a generalized grievance. Data Processing, an earlier standing case involving competitive economic harm under a specific statute, did not establish standing from an earnest interest in government. Levitt’s rejection of a citizen’s challenge to an allegedly unconstitutional judicial appointment showed that an express constitutional prohibition did not eliminate the injury requirement.

The possibility that no one could bring this particular suit did not alter the result. For the majority, that possibility reinforced Congress’s oversight and the electoral process as methods of control. Citizens could seek political change without an Article III remedy. The Court discussed historical secrecy and congressional reporting authority but reserved the accounting clause’s precise meaning; even an express statutory standing grant would remain subject to Article III.

On June 25, 1974 the Court reversed the Third Circuit, 5–4. It did not determine the accounting statute’s validity or reach the political-question ground. It also left unresolved an objection to a district judge’s participation in the en banc court, which was outside the question presented.

sections.title: Powell would limit taxpayer suits on broader institutional grounds
paragraphs: Justice Powell agreed with the judgment and most reasoning but would abandon Flast’s two-part nexus formula while preserving its settled Establishment Clause result. He thought the formula neither measured concrete adversity nor clearly separated constitutional and prudential restrictions. Richardson’s commitment was obvious and the accounting clause plausibly connected to spending, yet the formula excluded him.

Powell rejected the distinction between constitutional affirmative duties and prohibitions proposed by Justice Stewart. Either could support unlimited citizen suits, and grammar supplied no principled boundary. Such litigation could transfer supervision of elected branches to an insulated judiciary, produce selective review depending on who sued, and consume resources needed for individual and minority rights. He favored traditional prudential barriers and restrained expansion beyond the results of Flast and Baker, while recognizing a different situation for express statutory standing within Article III. These were his additional reasons, not the Court’s overruling of Flast.

sections.title: The dissenters see denial of information as a personal injury
paragraphs: Justice Douglas would affirm standing. He understood the accounting clause’s history as protecting public sovereignty and electoral control against fiscal secrecy. A taxpayer seeking the promised account sought enforcement of that protection, not abstract supervision. He contrasted the Constitution’s express allowance for secrecy in legislative journals with the accounting requirement and rejected political accountability as an adequate replacement for the disclosure protection.

Justice Stewart, joined by Justice Marshall, saw an ordinary right-and-duty dispute. Richardson alleged a personal entitlement to information and an affirmative governmental obligation; denial should allow litigation over whether that obligation existed. Whether the duty ran to Richardson, allowed secrecy exceptions, or implicated a political question belonged to later merits or justiciability analysis. Flast addressed spending challenges, not this claim. Stewart compared the request and denial to private obligations and Freedom of Information Act claims, emphasizing that widely shared injury was not necessarily insufficient. Political questions were outside the accepted Supreme Court question, and the Solicitor General agreed that standing would require a return to district court.

Justice Brennan’s dissent, printed in the companion Schlesinger case and expressly applying here, likewise separated injury in fact from reviewability and merits. Good-faith allegations of denied personal information and impairment of Richardson’s own informed voting sufficed, even if the claimed right ultimately failed. Extending Flast’s specialized formula to that dispute, Brennan argued, confused those distinct questions.
